subject: english-language

moments.title: Verbal Behavior
moments.body: 1957: Skinner's 'Verbal Behavior' published. Language is analysed as operant behaviour — verbal responses reinforced by listener consequences. Children learn language through stimulus-response conditioning, with reinforcement shaping correct production.
moments.takeaway: Skinner had built behaviourism into a major psychological framework (the Skinner box, operant conditioning with rats and pigeons). Verbal Behavior was the application to humans.

moments.title: Chomsky's review
moments.body: 1959: Chomsky's review (in the journal Language) attacks Verbal Behavior. The 'poverty of the stimulus' argument: children acquire language faster, more uniformly, and with more abstract structure than reinforcement can explain. The review is widely credited with effectively ending behaviourist accounts of language acquisition.
moments.takeaway: Skinner did not respond directly. The cognitive revolution was under way.

moments.title: Usage-based revival
moments.body: Late 20th and 21st-century usage-based linguistics (Michael Tomasello, Joan Bybee) revived parts of the behaviourist framework, without the strict conditioning model. Children learn language through actual usage, social interaction and frequency — but with strong cognitive and social mechanisms.
moments.takeaway: The debate between innate (Chomskyan) and usage-based approaches continues. Modern positions are usually hybrid.

now.title: Language acquisition now
now.body: Modern language acquisition research includes innate (UG), usage-based, social-pragmatic, and connectionist approaches. Skinner's pure behaviourism is largely abandoned, but operant conditioning principles still inform speech therapy and some teaching methods (autism early intervention).
now.open_questions: What's actually innate? Strong nativism (UG) and pure usage-based learning are both being refined. Most modern theorists accept some constraints on possible languages but argue about how much.

reflection: A psychology giant proposed a behaviourist account of language; a young linguist demolished it. The exchange is one of the foundational moments of cognitive science. Both Skinner and Chomsky shaped modern thinking about mind, language and learning — even where they were wrong, their formulations created the questions.
